Chapter Two: Facing the Problem of Suffering and Evil
Few questions cut as deeply as the ones about suffering and evil.
Why do innocent people have to go through pain? And why does it seem like evil sometimes gets the upper hand, while good people struggle just to get by?
These aren't just big, abstract questions—these are the kinds of things that keep us up at night, especially when tragedy hits close to home.
Picture a parent, sitting by their child's hospital bed. The beeping of machines, the white walls, the worry—they’re all there. And suddenly, all the usual answers just feel hollow.
The real question isn’t just, “Why me?” It’s, “How could a loving God let this happen?” For so many, this is the moment when faith really gets put to the test.
When we start searching for understanding, we often talk to people who’ve spent their lives wrestling with these questions. Some folks point to the idea of free will—saying that for love to be real, we have to be free to choose, even if that means some will choose wrong.
That doesn’t make suffering any easier, but it does give us a way to think about why a world without pain might also be a world without genuine love or real choices.
Others look at suffering and see how it can sometimes lead to growth. Think about someone who’s lost everything—a job, maybe even their sense of who they are.
Sometimes, after all that loss, they find a deeper connection with their family, or they figure out what really matters to them. Or maybe you know someone who survived a tough illness, and after that, became the person everyone turns to for comfort.
But let’s be honest—these explanations don’t magically take away the pain. For a lot of us, the most honest thing we can do is admit that some suffering will always be a mystery.
Maybe God has reasons we just can’t see. Sometimes, that’s comforting. Other times, it’s just plain frustrating.
It’s a reminder that faith isn’t always about having all the answers. Sometimes, it means living with questions that don’t get wrapped up neatly.
And yet, even in the middle of suffering, people find these surprising moments of grace.
Like a nurse who offers a gentle word, or a friend who just sits quietly with you, or a whole community that shows up when you need them most.
These small acts of love—they’re proof that goodness can shine through, even in the darkest times.
Over time, you start to see that the presence of evil and suffering doesn’t have to mean God is absent.
Instead, it can be a wake-up call—a reminder to fight injustice, to comfort those who are hurting, and to keep searching for hope, even when it feels impossible.
For many, struggling with suffering actually becomes a core part of faith.
It shapes you. It makes you more compassionate, more resilient, and more aware of the needs around you.
